title: Macros, object-like/function-like macros and conditional compilation
learningObjectives: Explain that preprocessing handles directives before the compiler parses the resulting translation unit.
Define and use object-like macros for symbolic constants and configuration switches while distinguishing them from typed const objects and enum constants.
Write function-like macros with fully parenthesized parameters and replacement expressions to avoid precedence errors.
Recognize repeated evaluation, side effects and type-checking limitations in function-like macros.
Use #if, #ifdef, #ifndef, #elif and #else to include or exclude source text based on preprocessing conditions.
Apply stringizing and token-pasting only when they solve a clear preprocessing problem, and inspect preprocessed output when diagnosing macro expansion.
prerequisites: CL1.3 C program structure and preprocessing
CL3.4 Operator precedence and expression grouping

understand.concept: The C preprocessor processes directives such as #include, #define and conditional-compilation blocks before the compiler performs the language's normal parsing and semantic analysis. A macro is token substitution, not a typed function. Object-like macros replace an identifier; function-like macros substitute arguments into a replacement token sequence.
understand.whyItMatters: Macros support header guards, configuration, conditional compilation and carefully designed abstractions. But they can create surprising precedence, repeated evaluation and debugging problems because their expansion happens before normal C type checking.
understand.analogy: A macro resembles a text template that is expanded before the final document is reviewed.
understand.analogyLimit: Unlike a C function, a macro does not create a function call boundary, has no parameter types, and may evaluate an argument more than once. Text-template intuition alone is not enough to reason about tokenization.

explain.narrative:
A directive begins with # at the start of a preprocessing directive. `#define LIMIT 100` defines an object-like macro. A function-like macro requires the opening parenthesis immediately after the macro name: `#define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x))`. Parenthesize each parameter occurrence and the whole replacement expression, but remember that this does not prevent repeated evaluation: SQUARE(i++) is unsafe because i++ appears twice. Prefer an inline function when ordinary typed evaluation is suitable.

Conditional compilation selects source text before C compilation. `#if` expressions are integer constant expressions after macro replacement; `#ifdef NAME` tests whether a macro exists. Use `#undef` deliberately, keep macro names distinctive, and do not attempt to create runtime branches with preprocessor directives. The `#` and `##` operators perform stringizing and token pasting within function-like macro replacement lists.

examples.title: A precedence-safe macro and a safer inline alternative
examples.explanation: The macro parameter and replacement expression are parenthesized, so SQUARE(a + 1) expands as ((a + 1) * (a + 1)). The inline function has one typed parameter evaluation and is safer when an argument may have side effects.

examples.title: Select a build-time feature with conditional compilation
examples.explanation: The preprocessor chooses one branch before compilation. Changing APP_DIAGNOSTICS changes which source text reaches the compiler; this is not a runtime if statement.

practise.guidedTask: Expand SQUARE(a + 1) by hand and compare it with an intentionally unparenthesized macro. Then replace the macro call with square_int and explain the difference for an expression such as i++.
practise.independentTask: Create a header configuration macro that conditionally enables diagnostics. Add one function-like macro with safe parentheses, then document one argument expression that must not be passed because it would be evaluated more than once.
hints: The preprocessor performs token substitution before C parsing and type checking.
Use parentheses around every parameter occurrence and around the entire replacement expression.
Parentheses do not prevent repeated argument evaluation or side effects.
Prefer a function or inline function when you need type checking and single evaluation.
Use #ifdef to test whether a macro is defined; use #if when testing its numeric value.
Inspect compiler preprocessed output when an expansion is confusing; keep macros small and narrowly scoped.

questions.prompt: When does macro replacement normally occur?
options: During preprocessing, before the compiler parses the resulting translation unit.
At runtime on every function call.
Only after linking.
After the program exits.
questions.answer: During preprocessing, before the compiler parses the resulting translation unit.
questions.explanation: Macro directives are processed before the compiler parses and type-checks the expanded C source.

questions.prompt: Which macro definition correctly groups both the argument and result?
options: #define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x))
#define SQUARE(x) x * x
#define SQUARE(x) (x * x +)
#define SQUARE x*x
questions.explanation: Parenthesizing each parameter and the full expression protects grouping when the macro is substituted into larger expressions.

questions.prompt: Why is `SQUARE(i++)` unsafe for the macro shown in the lesson?
options: The argument expression appears twice and can be evaluated more than once.
The preprocessor always rejects increment operators.
Macros cannot accept variables.
The multiplication operator is not allowed in macros.
questions.answer: The argument expression appears twice and can be evaluated more than once.
questions.explanation: The replacement contains two occurrences of x, so i++ can be evaluated twice and create an unsequenced modification problem.

options: Whether FEATURE is defined as a macro.
Whether FEATURE is nonzero at runtime.
Whether a function named FEATURE exists.
Whether a header file is installed.
questions.answer: Whether FEATURE is defined as a macro.
questions.explanation: ifdef checks macro definition state during preprocessing, not a runtime value.

questions.prompt: When is an ordinary function usually preferable to a function-like macro?
options: When typed parameters and single evaluation are important.
When the replacement must run before compilation.
When a directive must choose source text at build time.
When stringizing a token is required.
questions.answer: When typed parameters and single evaluation are important.
questions.explanation: A function provides typed parameters and evaluates each argument expression once as part of the call.
